q: Which of these is outside a certified personal trainer's scope of practice?
o: Diagnosing the cause of a client's knee pain
e: Diagnosing or treating pain and disease belongs to medical professionals. A CPT assesses, programmes, gives general nutritional information and refers out beyond that.

q: How is a fitness professional's scope of practice mainly defined in the US?
o: By federal legislation written specifically for personal trainers
By the certifying body's own rules, which carry no legal weight
Through association to adjacent allied health professions and their rules
By the waiver the client signs before the first session
e: There is no specific governmental regulation of fitness professionals in the US and many other countries. The boundary comes from adjacent professions, whose own rules stop CPTs performing certain health-related activities.

q: Who may legally provide nutrition counselling?
o: Any certified personal trainer, wherever they happen to practise
Only a licensed physician, in every region
In some regions only a registered dietitian; in others, anyone
Any CPT whose client has signed a liability disclaimer
e: Scope varies by country and region. In some places only a registered dietitian nutritionist may counsel on nutrition; in others no licence is required, so the CPT must know current local law.

q: Which certification must a CPT hold current and be able to act on in an emergency?
o: First aid alone, without resuscitation training
e: Holding current CPR and AED certification, and responding appropriately in emergencies, is explicitly within scope. The others are optional additions, not requirements.

q: Under the NASM Code of Professional Conduct, which belongs to the 'honesty, integrity and lawfulness' area?
o: Maintaining a hygienic and professional appearance
Carrying adequate liability insurance and keeping progress notes
Storing and disposing of client records securely
Upholding copyright, trademark and intellectual property law
e: Honesty, integrity and lawfulness covers liability insurance, progress notes, truthful advertising, accurate financial records and compliance with harassment and discrimination law. Appearance sits under professionalism, records under confidentiality, copyright under legal and ethical.

q: What can follow a failure to comply with the Code of Professional Conduct?
o: A mandatory retake of the certification exam within 12 months
Revocation of the certification, and possibly legal action
A fine paid to the certifying body
A written warning held on file by the employer
e: The stated consequence is revocation of the certification, with legal action possible in serious cases.

q: A client says 'I feel like everyone is staring at me.' Which barrier is this?
e: Social physique anxiety is anxiety about physical appearance, or about how the client believes others see and judge them. Responses include comfortable clothing, quieter areas and alternative ways to participate.

q: Which barrier is described as the largest, used to explain lack of exercise, poor eating and poor stress management alike?
e: Time is the largest barrier and is used to explain poor eating and poor stress management as well. The approach is to find where there is genuinely no wiggle room and design around it, often placing exercise first thing in the morning or immediately after work.

q: Why does an unrealistic goal itself become a barrier?
o: It cannot be written in specific, measurable terms
The client feels defeated and stops
It sets a timeline the trainer cannot commit to
It cannot be tracked with objective data over time
e: Clients get too ambitious, then frustrated. Believing they are not progressing leads to feeling defeated and stopping, so goals need flexibility, progression and celebrated milestones.

q: A client appears not to care about starting. Which barrier is this?
e: Ambivalence looks like not caring but the root cause is mixed feelings. The response is to talk through the benefits of exercise and the negative effects of sedentary living.

q: How is convenience described as a barrier?
o: Objective, and measurable in travel minutes
Relevant only to clients who train at a gym
A physical barrier rather than one of perception
e: Convenience is entirely subjective. Clients accept considerable inconvenience where they believe the value is exceptional, so the fix is options: home, a lunch hour, or between other activities.

q: Believing you lack the time or energy is which type of barrier?
o: A physical barrier, since low energy has a physical cause
A barrier of perception, not a physical one
A mixed barrier, combining physical and perceived elements
Not a barrier, because it cannot be measured
e: Barriers are physical, perceptual or mixed. A perceived barrier can feel entirely physical to the person experiencing it, so it should not be dismissed. Mixed describes competing life demands, such as a single parent balancing career and children.

q: In the study cited, gym members who predicted three or more sessions a week actually averaged:
e: People overestimate how often they will exercise. Members predicting three or more sessions averaged 1.39 a week.

q: 'I will always work out during my lunch break' is an example of:
e: Implementation intentions drive behaviour by naming a cue for action. Coping planning anticipates barriers; self-monitoring tracks behaviour after the fact.

q: Which cognitive strategy involves saying 'stop' out loud when negative thought patterns appear?
e: The stopping technique breaks the cycle of negative thinking. Reverse listing is the complementary one: identify the negative inner narrative and replace it with positive statements.

q: A client mentally rehearses a session focusing on making their technique as close to perfect as possible. This is:
e: Mental imagery has three subsets: appearance imagery (appearance or health outcomes), energy imagery (energy and stress relief) and technique imagery (focus on technique).

q: When does positive feedback and praise matter most for building self-efficacy?
o: In the early stages of behaviour change
Once the client reaches their outcome goal
e: Praise on any improvement in any metric builds confidence through little victories, and it matters most in the early stages of behaviour change.

q: For a client in the contemplation stage, serious planning may be premature. What is suggested instead?
o: Setting a demanding outcome goal to create urgency
Reviewing barriers already experienced and planning together for their recurrence
Waiting until the client reaches the action stage before discussing barriers
Beginning formal fitness testing to establish a baseline
e: Serious planning may not suit a client still weighing the decision. Reviewing barriers that have already arisen keeps the conversation concrete without demanding commitment.

q: What is the stated primary goal of the fitness professional?
o: To maximise measurable strength and body composition gains
To help people adopt exercise and stay active long term
To retain each client for as many paid sessions as possible
To correct every postural distortion found at assessment
e: Adoption plus long-term maintenance. That is why understanding how ready a client is to change matters so much.

q: In NASM's wording, SMART stands for:
e: NASM uses Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic, Timely. Failing any one criterion means the goal will likely fail to meet the client's needs.

q: 'Win a 10K race within one year' is which kind of goal?
e: An outcome goal is the consequence, the final achievement. Process goals are the daily and weekly steps, such as jogging an hour three days a week.

q: Why do process goals enhance self-efficacy?
o: They are easier to measure than outcome goals
They remove the need for an outcome goal
They are set by the trainer rather than the client
e: Once an outcome goal is set, process goals are created that speak to how it will be achieved. Each small win on them builds confidence.

q: What distinguishes 'Attainable' from 'Realistic' in NASM's SMART?
o: Nothing; NASM treats the two as interchangeable
Attainable concerns the level of challenge; Realistic concerns relevance
Attainable concerns the time frame; Realistic concerns how progress is measured
Attainable applies to outcome goals, Realistic to process goals
e: Attainable is about calibration: too easy and the client will not put in sufficient effort, too challenging and they get discouraged. Realistic asks whether it fits this client's lifestyle, not merely whether it is technically possible.

q: Goals sit at the crossroads of how and why. What is the 'why'?
e: The why is the client's values; the how is the way the goal will be achieved. Both professional and client should be able to verbalise why a goal matters.

q: When should goal setting begin?
o: After the first formal fitness assessment
After four weeks, once a training habit exists
Once the PAR-Q+ has cleared the client
e: Goal setting starts at the first meeting and begins with long-term goals rooted in the client's values. Useful openers are what they want to accomplish in six months, and what success in fitness looks like to them.

q: What does the PAR-Q+ answer?
o: Who the person is and how they live
Whether it is safe to be more active
What their body fat percentage and BMI are
Which energy system their training should target
e: The PAR-Q+ is the pre-participation health screen: it answers safety. The Lifestyle and Health History Questionnaire answers who the person is. They are used together.

q: How many general health questions does the PAR-Q+ (2024) contain?
e: Seven general questions. All 'no' clears the client, who then signs the participant declaration. Any 'yes' routes to follow-up pages on specific chronic conditions.

q: A client answers 'yes' to a PAR-Q+ question. What happens?
o: They are barred from exercising until a physician clears them
They complete follow-up pages on chronic conditions
They sign the participant declaration regardless
The trainer decides on the spot whether to proceed
e: Follow-up pages address specific chronic conditions and can require medical clearance or referral before starting.

q: Which section of the Lifestyle and Health History Questionnaire covers extended sitting, repetitive movements and heeled footwear?
e: The Occupation section captures the job itself plus extended sitting, repetitive movements and heeled footwear, all of which shape posture.

q: Which pulse site should be avoided when measuring a client's resting heart rate?
e: Reaching for a client's neck causes discomfort and spikes the reading, pressure can occlude blood flow to the brain, and it can induce a vasovagal response producing a large drop in heart rate and blood pressure.

q: Why should a pulse never be taken with the thumb?
o: It is too short to reach the artery reliably
It has a strong pulse of its own
It is less sensitive than the first two fingers
It compresses the artery and distorts the count
e: The thumb carries a strong pulse of its own, so the risk is counting the assessor's rate rather than the client's. It is also more sensitive than the fingers, not less.

q: What is the best method for obtaining resting heart rate?
o: Immediately after the client's first training session
First thing in the morning, taken by the client on waking
At the end of a thorough warm-up, once the rate has settled
At any point after the client has been seated for five minutes
e: Resting heart rate is lowest and least disturbed on waking, so the client sits up out of bed and takes it themselves, ideally averaged over three or five days. Wearable continuous heart rate devices are relatively accurate and acceptable.

q: Which counting duration gives the most accurate resting heart rate?
e: A full 60 seconds is most accurate. The shorter the count, the greater the error introduced by multiplying up.

q: What does the systolic number measure?
o: Force on the vessel walls between heartbeats
Force on the vessel walls when the heart contracts
The volume of blood pumped per minute
e: Systolic, the top number, is the force when the heart contracts. Diastolic, the bottom number, is the force between heartbeats as blood returns to the heart.

q: What are Korotkoff sounds?
o: Blood bouncing off the vessel walls
The heart valves opening and closing
Breath sounds carried through the chest wall
e: Korotkoff sounds are heard through the stethoscope as blood bounces off the vessel walls. The first prominent sound is systolic; the last sound before silence is diastolic.

q: At what rate should cuff pressure be released when taking blood pressure?
e: Release slowly, about 2 mmHg per second, having inflated above the expected systolic, around 150 to 160 mmHg. Releasing faster risks missing the first and last sounds.

q: Where should blood pressure be measured, and why?
o: At the wrist, because it sits furthest from the heart
Level with the heart, because pressure differs with body position
On the right upper arm, because the aorta leaves the heart on that side
Anywhere convenient, since body position does not change the reading
e: Pressure varies with position relative to the heart, so the measurement site must be level with it. Use the left upper arm, rested on a box or desk.

q: Normal blood pressure is defined as:
e: Under 120 systolic and under 80 diastolic. Elevated measurements are hypertension, which has stages depending on how elevated.

q: Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Peripheral resistance increases when the arteries are:
o: Carrying a greater volume of blood
e: A narrower vessel resists flow more. Constriction raises peripheral resistance; dilation lowers it.

q: A resting heart rate below 60 bpm is called:
e: Bradycardia is below 60, tachycardia is above 100, and the untrained adult range is approximately 60 to 100 bpm.

q: Stroke volume is calculated as:
o: Cardiac output divided by heart rate squared
e: End-diastolic volume is the filled volume before contraction; end-systolic volume is the residual after ejection. Typical adult stroke volume is roughly 75 to 80 mL per beat.

q: A well-conditioned client has a slower than normal resting heart rate. Why?
o: Their resting metabolic rate is lower
Training improved the heart's ability to pump
They carry less total blood volume
Their arteries are permanently dilated, lowering resistance
e: A stronger, more efficient pump moves the same volume in fewer beats, so resting heart rate falls.

q: Which body fat measurement method is the gold standard?
e: Hydrostatic weighing is the gold standard, and most body-fat-and-health charts were produced with it. DEXA can be very accurate but is a clinical tool, not the reference against which the others are judged.

q: The main source of inaccuracy in bioelectrical impedance is:
o: Skin temperature at the contact points
e: Impedance readings depend heavily on how hydrated the client is, which is why the method gives only a good indication rather than a reliable figure.

q: Skinfold calipers carry roughly what error against hydrostatic weighing?
e: About 3.5%, and the inaccuracy is mostly user error, which means practice reduces it. That makes calipers practical in a fitness setting.

q: What is the most common error in taking a skinfold measurement?
o: Marking the site with a grease pencil before measuring
Pinching only skin instead of the underlying fat
Leaving less than 15 seconds between repeat measurements
Taking more than one measurement at the same site
e: The fat must be gripped and pulled clear of the muscle, with the fingers spread two to three inches apart. Repeating a site and marking it are correct practice, not errors.

q: How soon should you read the calipers after releasing pressure?
e: Read within one to two seconds. Leaving the calipers on compresses the fat and changes the reading. Wait at least 15 seconds before repeating a site.

q: Two consecutive measurements at a skinfold site must agree within:
e: Two consecutive readings at a site must fall within one to two millimetres of each other, otherwise the site is repeated until they do.

q: In the three-site skinfold protocol for men, which sites are used?
e: Men: chest (diagonal), abdomen (vertical), thigh (vertical). Women: triceps (vertical), suprailiac (diagonal), thigh (vertical).

q: Which fold direction is correct for the male chest site?
o: Vertical, halfway between the armpit crease and the nipple
Diagonal, halfway between the armpit crease and the nipple
e: The male chest fold is diagonal and sits halfway between the crease of the armpit and the nipple. The abdomen and thigh folds are the vertical ones.

q: Waist-to-hip ratio is calculated as:
o: Hip circumference divided by waist circumference
Waist circumference divided by hip circumference
e: Waist divided by hips. An apple shape, where the waist measures larger than the hips, is associated with negative health risks because more fat is distributed around the organs.

q: Where is the waist measured for waist-to-hip ratio?
o: At the level of the umbilicus
At the most narrow part of the torso
e: The most narrow part of the torso, found with the client standing with arms out. The hips are measured at the area of largest circumference, taking the buttocks into account.

q: When during the breath should the waist measurement be taken?
o: At full inhalation, with the chest expanded
At the end of the breath
While the client holds the breath in
At the point of maximal exhalation
e: Measuring at the end of the breath avoids both an inflated chest and a forced squeeze. Use a non-elastic tape pulled snug but not too tight.

q: What are the five kinetic chain checkpoints?
o: Foot and ankle, calf, thigh, trunk, arms
Foot and ankle, knee, LPHC, shoulders, head and neck
Foot and ankle, knee, wrist, scapulae, head and cervical spine
e: Foot and ankle, knee, LPHC, shoulders, head and neck, each checked from three views: anterior, posterior and lateral.

q: A static postural assessment should end in three judgements. Which set?
o: Height, weight and body mass index
Distortion syndrome, overactive and underactive muscles
Range of motion at the hip, knee and shoulder
Pain scores, stiffness scores and self-reported weakness
e: The point is to reach conclusions rather than record findings, because the overactive and underactive judgements are what the programme is built from.

q: Flat feet with adducted and internally rotated knees, giving a knock-kneed appearance, describes which distortion pattern?
o: A combination of upper-extremity and lumbo-pelvic-hip complex
e: That is the lower-extremity pattern. Stretch the calves and adductor complex; strengthen the foot and ankle stabilisers (anterior tibialis) and the gluteals.

q: In the LPHC distortion pattern, which muscles are stretched and which strengthened?
o: Stretch hip flexors, strengthen gluteals and core
e: Sitting leaves the hip flexors shortened and tight and the gluteals and deep core lengthened and weak. Stretch the hip flexors, strengthen the gluteals and deep abdominals.

q: What is the practical tell for anterior pelvic tilt?
o: The belt line, higher at the back than the front
The position of the shoulder blades against the wall
Head position relative to the wall
e: A belt line higher at the back and lower at the front indicates anterior tilt, which comes with a hyperextended lower back, also called excessive lumbar lordosis.

q: Rounded shoulders and upper back with a forward head produces:
e: That is the upper-extremity pattern, common in people who sit at a computer or drive for long periods. It can cause shoulder pain, neck pain and headaches.

q: In the upper-extremity pattern, what should be strengthened?
o: The middle back and rotator cuff
The hip flexors and the deep core
e: Strengthen the rhomboids, mid and lower trapezius and the rotator cuff; stretch the chest and upper trapezius. What is held short becomes overactive and needs stretching, what is held long becomes underactive and needs strengthening.

q: Why is a static postural assessment alone incomplete?
o: It examines only three of the five kinetic chain checkpoints
Posture is dynamic and constantly adjusts to the body's demands
It cannot identify overactive or underactive muscles
e: A still standing posture says nothing about how the body organises itself under load. The overhead squat assessment is usually the first dynamic test and acts as a total body scan.

q: What does the OHSA evaluate in one movement?
o: Ankle mobility and knee alignment, but nothing above the waist
Dynamic posture, core stability, flexibility, coordination
Cardiorespiratory fitness and recovery heart rate
e: All four at once, which is why it counts as a total body scan. Impairments it reveals, such as knee valgus or limited ankle mobility, can predict injury risk and direct the programme.

q: What is the correct starting position for the OHSA?
o: Feet hip-width apart, shoes on, hands resting on the hip bones
Feet shoulder-width and straight, barefoot, arms overhead
Feet wide and turned out, arms folded across the chest
Feet together, arms hanging by the sides
e: Feet shoulder-width and pointing straight on a flat surface, feet and ankles neutral, barefoot so the foot and ankle are visible, arms raised overhead with the elbows straight.

q: How many repetitions are performed, and from which views?
o: Five, from the front and the side
One, from the side, at a self-selected depth
e: Five repetitions, squatting to thighs parallel and returning, modifying depth if needed, observed anteriorly and laterally.

q: Arms falling forward during the overhead squat indicates:
o: Weakness in the front of the shoulder with overactivity across the upper back
Overactivity in the front of the shoulder, weakness in the upper back
Overactivity in the hamstrings and calves, limiting squat depth
Restricted ankle dorsiflexion pulling the torso forward
e: Ideally the arms stay vertical as an extension of the torso, biceps by the ears. Falling forward means the front is pulling and the back is not holding, so the fix is flexibility through the front plus activation and strengthening through the upper back.

q: What is the ideal relationship between shin and torso in the lateral view of an overhead squat?
o: The torso vertical regardless of the shin
The shin vertical regardless of the torso
e: A parallel line between shin and torso. Excessive forward lean suggests weakness in the spinal muscles, spinal column and hips, with possible overactivity in the front of the hip.

q: How is knee buckling judged?
o: By the knees touching at the bottom of the squat
By the kneecaps falling inside the big toes
By the heels lifting off the floor
By the feet turning out beyond 15 degrees
e: Middle of the kneecaps falling inside the big toes. It indicates overactivity in the inner thigh and weakness in the outer hip.

q: What is the corrective approach for knees buckling in?
o: Strengthen the inner thigh and stretch the outer hip
Strengthen the outer hip, stretch the inner thigh
Strengthen the calves and stretch the hamstrings
Strengthen the quadriceps and stretch the hip flexors
e: Overactive tissue gets flexibility and self-myofascial work, underactive tissue gets activation and strengthening. Here the inner thigh is overactive and the outer hip underactive, so foam rolling and static stretching go to the adductors.

q: How should OHSA findings be communicated to a client?
o: As a list of faults for the client to work through
Tactfully, framed around movement safety and efficiency
In clinical terms, so the client understands the exact diagnosis
Only once the programme is written, to avoid alarming them
e: Framing around safety and efficiency keeps the client engaged rather than defensive. Naming a diagnosis would also fall outside scope.

q: The YMCA 3-minute step test is scored on:
o: Blood pressure measured immediately after the test
e: Scoring uses recovery heart rate against age and sex norms, rated on a seven-point scale from very poor to excellent. A lower recovery heart rate is better.

q: What are the three components of the human movement system?
e: The nervous system controls the muscles, the muscular system moves, the skeletal system determines how the joints move. Nerves move muscles; muscles move bones.

q: What is a muscle imbalance?
o: Two opposing muscles of unequal size
A less than optimal length-tension relationship
Any asymmetry between the left and right sides
A muscle that fatigues faster than its neighbours
e: The short, overactive muscle has too much tone and pulls the bones toward its side; the lengthened, underactive one allows that pull. The joint then sits in a less than optimal position, increasing stress in the area.

q: What does regional interdependence mean?
o: Joints depend on other joints for movement
Muscles depend on their tendons to transmit force
Each body region can be trained in isolation from the others
A joint's range of motion depends only on the muscles crossing it
e: Because joints depend on each other, human movement system dysfunction works like a stack of dominoes: an imbalance in one area tends to create imbalances throughout.

q: In the domino chain from the ground up, subtalar pronation and a collapsed arch lead first to:
e: Collapsed arch, then internal tibial rotation, then femoral rotation, then that hip drops and internally rotates, and what happens at the hip also happens at the shoulders.

q: Which is NOT one of the five functions of the skeletal system?
o: Providing the structure from which movement is created
e: The five are: shape and form, support and protection of organs, structure for movement, blood production, mineral storage.

q: Which division of the skeleton contains the skull, rib cage and vertebral column?
e: The axial skeleton has approximately 80 bones. The appendicular has approximately 126: arms, legs and pelvic girdle.

q: Which cells break down and remove old bone tissue?
e: Osteoclasts break down and remove old bone; osteoblasts form new bone. The two together are remodelling.

q: The patella is an example of which bone type?
e: Sesamoid bones are small and embedded in a joint capsule or where a tendon passes over a joint. Carpals are short, vertebrae irregular, the sternum flat, the femur long.

q: A groove allowing soft tissue such as muscle, tendon or ligament to pass through is a:
e: A sulcus is a groove and a fossa is a flattened or indented portion; both are depressions. Processes are projections where tendons and ligaments attach.

q: Trochanters are found at the top of which bone?
e: Trochanters sit at the top of the femur and are attachment sites for hip musculature. Tubercles sit at the top of the humerus for shoulder musculature.

q: Total peak bone mass is reached at approximately what age?
e: Peak bone mass is reached around 30, stays stable from 30 to 50, then declines, which is why osteoporosis risk rises in older individuals.

q: Which pair is NOT weight-bearing exercise?
e: Swimming and cycling still build muscle and cardiovascular health, and contraction force across bones carries some benefit, but they do not force the body to work against gravity.

q: Approximately what proportion of the body's joints are synovial?
e: About 80 percent, and they have the greatest capacity for motion. They are characterised by the absence of fibrous or cartilaginous tissue directly connecting the bones.

q: What does synovial fluid do?
o: Connects the bones to one another
Lubricates the joint surfaces and nourishes the cartilage
Forms the cartilage padding on the ends of the articulating bones
e: It resembles egg white and works like engine oil, secreted within the capsule from the synovial membrane. It reduces excessive wear and feeds the cartilage cells.

q: The elbow and knee are given as examples of which type of synovial joint?
e: Hinge joints are uniaxial, moving predominantly in one direction like a door hinge. The knee is a modified hinge, because it can slide and then roll.

q: Which joint type is the most mobile, moving in all three directions?
e: Ball-and-socket joints, the shoulder and the hip, are the most mobile. Gliding joints are non-axial and the simplest, moving back and forth or side to side.

q: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is which type?
e: In a saddle joint one bone resembles a saddle and the other straddles it like a rider, giving back-and-forth and side-to-side movement with limited rotation.

q: Which two proteins make up ligaments, and what does each contribute?
o: Actin for strength and myosin for recoil
Collagen for tensile strength, elastin for recoil
Keratin for strength and elastin for recoil
Collagen for recoil and elastin for tensile strength
e: Collagen gives the ability to withstand tension; elastin gives flexibility and elastic recoil to withstand bending and twisting. The ACL is meagre in elastin and predominantly collagen.

q: Ligaments heal slowly. Why?
o: They are made of cartilage rather than fibrous tissue
e: Poor blood supply means slow repair and slow adaptation, which is true of tendons too. Ligaments are in fact mostly collagen, and they do supply sensory input that aids proprioception.

q: What is the difference between osteokinematics and arthrokinematics?
o: Osteokinematics is joint movement we cannot see; arthrokinematics is bone movement we can see
Osteokinematics is how the bones move; arthrokinematics is what happens inside the joint
They are two words for the same thing
Osteokinematics applies only to synovial joints
e: Osteokinematics is the visible vocabulary of flexion, extension and the rest; arthrokinematics is the roll, slide and spin inside the joint. Both are necessary for normal movement.

q: Which arthrokinematic motion is described as a tire rolling on the street?
e: Roll is a tyre rolling on the street. Slide, or glide, is a bicycle tyre skidding; spin is twisting the lid off a jar, as in forearm pronation and supination.

q: Which vertebrae are the largest bones in the spinal column?
e: The lumbar vertebrae, L1 to L5, support most of the body's weight and attach to many back muscles. That is also why the lumbar spine is often a location of pain.

q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there, and what distinguishes them?
o: Twelve, each articulating with a rib
e: T1 to T12, each articulating with a rib to form the rear anchor of the rib cage. They are larger than cervical vertebrae and increase in size top to bottom.

q: What do intervertebral discs do?
o: Absorb shock and allow the spine to move
Protect the spinal cord from direct impact
e: Intervertebral discs are fibrous cartilage sitting between the vertebrae. They absorb shock and allow the spine to move; protecting the cord is the job of the vertebral column itself.

q: Neutral spine is best defined as:
o: A completely straight spinal column with no curves
The position of least load on the vertebrae
Maximum lumbar lordosis, with the pelvis tilted forward
The position the spine takes when lying supine
e: Viewed from the side the spinal column is curved, partially resembling an S. Neutral is the optimal arrangement of those curves, the position of least load and best support for functional movement.

q: The oblique is ___ to the rectus abdominis.
e: Lateral means toward the outside of the body, medial near the middle. So the oblique is lateral to the rectus abdominis, and the rectus abdominis is medial to the oblique.

q: Which term means positioned on the opposite side of the body?
e: Contralateral is opposite side, ipsilateral is same side. Proximal is nearest the centre or point of reference, distal is farthest.

q: Lying face down on the belly, as in a plank or Superman, is:
e: Prone is face down. Supine is lying on the spine, face up, as in a crunch or bench press.

q: Biomechanics is defined as:
o: The study of how muscles contract at the cellular level
The study of forces placed upon the body, using physics
The measurement of body composition and its associated health risks
The study of how the body produces and uses energy
e: Biomechanics applies the principles of physics to how internal and external forces interact within a living body.

q: Which motions occur in the sagittal plane?
e: The sagittal plane bisects the body into left and right halves and carries flexion and extension. Sagittal means arrow.

q: The frontal plane bisects the body into which halves, and carries which motions?
o: Left and right; flexion and extension
Front and back; abduction, adduction, lateral flexion, eversion and inversion
Top and bottom; rotation, horizontal abduction and adduction, pronation and supination
Front and back; rotation, pronation and supination
e: The frontal plane, also called coronal after the coronal suture of the skull, splits front from back. The list in option three belongs to the transverse plane.

q: Which motions belong to the transverse plane?
o: Rotation, horizontal abduction and adduction, pronation and supination
Abduction, adduction, lateral flexion, eversion, inversion and scapular elevation
Dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, eversion and inversion
e: The transverse plane bisects the body into top and bottom halves, and transverse means across. The longer list belongs to the frontal plane.

q: Flexion is defined as:
o: A movement away from the midline of the body
A bending movement that decreases the angle between two segments
A movement toward the midline of the body
A straightening movement that increases the angle between segments
e: Flexion decreases the relative angle, extension increases it. Movement toward and away from the midline is adduction and abduction, which belong to the frontal plane.

q: Bringing the top of the foot closer to the shin is:
e: Dorsal is the upper side, so dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot. Plantar is the sole, so plantar flexion points the foot away.

q: Hip flexion occurs two ways. The hip hinge is which?
o: Femur on pelvis, with the pelvis static and the femur swinging
Pelvis on femur, the femur static and the hips moving over it
Both occurring at once, which is why it is called a hinge
Neither; the hip hinge is a form of hip extension
e: Both routes decrease the angle between femur and pelvis. Femur on pelvis moves the leg; pelvis on femur, the hip hinge, moves the pelvis over a fixed femur.

q: What is hyperextension?
o: Extension of a joint through its full normal range
Extension beyond the joint's normal limit
Extension of the spine specifically, as in a back bend
e: The term is reserved for movement past the normal limit of extension. Extension through the available range, however large, is not hyperextension.

q: Eversion of the foot is:
o: Lifting the medial portion and standing on the lateral edge
Collapsing the arch onto the medial edge of the foot
e: Eversion collapses the arch onto the medial portion, equivalently lifting the lateral portion off the floor. Inversion is the opposite: lifting the medial portion and standing on the lateral edge.

q: Turning the forearm from palm down to palm up is:
e: Radioulnar supination goes palm down to palm up; pronation goes palm up to palm down. Radioulnar refers to the radius and ulna.

q: A chest fly starts with the elbows out wide and moves them inward. Which motion is that?
e: Horizontal adduction moves the arm horizontally from lateral toward anterior. Do not confuse it with pressing motions using shoulder flexion and extension, which are sagittal and keep the elbows close to the torso.

q: With the feet planted, rotating the hips to the right produces:
o: External rotation of the right hip and internal rotation of the left
External rotation of the left hip and internal rotation of the right
e: Rotating right externally rotates the left hip and internally rotates the right. Rotating left reverses it.

q: Pronation of the foot and ankle complex combines:
o: Inversion, plantar flexion and forefoot adduction
Eversion, plantar flexion and forefoot adduction
e: Pronation is eversion (frontal), dorsiflexion (sagittal) and forefoot abduction (transverse). Supination is the mirror: inversion, plantar flexion, forefoot adduction.

q: In walking and running, which phase involves pronation?
o: Force production, as the foot pushes off
e: Pronation happens during force reduction, supination during force production as the foot pushes off.

q: Isolated scapular movements are called translations because:
o: They occur in two planes at once
They do not rotate around a fixed axis
They transmit force from the arm into the spine
They occur only when the arm is overhead
e: A translation is movement without rotation about a fixed axis, which is what separates scapular motion from joint motions such as flexion or abduction. The four are retraction, protraction, elevation and depression.

q: Why is walking a multiplanar movement?
o: The arms swing in the frontal plane while the legs work sagittally
The hips and knees work sagittally while the torso rotates
Both feet leave the ground at some point in the cycle
The head moves in three directions to maintain balance
e: Sagittal below, transverse above, because power is generated by rotating. Training across all three planes prevents imbalances; a lunge with rotation is the multiplanar training example.

q: Which are the three types of muscle tissue?
e: Cardiac and smooth make up the heart and internal organ tissues. Skeletal muscle matters most for a fitness professional.

q: The muscular system links which two systems?
e: It generates internal tension that, under the nervous system's control, manipulates the bones to produce movement.

q: Which layer of connective tissue directly surrounds an entire muscle?
e: From outside in: fascia, epimysium (whole muscle), perimysium (each fascicle), endomysium (individual fibres), sarcolemma (the fibre's plasma membrane).

q: What is the functional unit of the muscular system?
e: The sarcomere is the repeating section of overlapping myofilaments and the physical site of contraction. Its meeting point is the Z line.

q: Actin and myosin are, respectively:
o: The thick and the thin filament
The thin and the thick filament
Two names for the same filament
e: Actin is the thin filament, myosin the thick. Sliding filament theory says they slide past one another to shorten the sarcomere and the muscle.

q: What is a motor unit?
o: One motor neuron and the fibres it stimulates
A group of synergistic muscles acting together
e: The neuromuscular junction is where the nerve joins the muscle fibre, and the small gap there is the synapse.

q: In excitation-contraction coupling, which neurotransmitter crosses the synapse?
e: Acetylcholine is released into the junction to help the impulse cross. Sodium and potassium facilitate the impulse travelling down the neuron.

q: What does the sarcoplasmic reticulum release to trigger contraction?
e: The impulse travels into the muscle and stimulates the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium, which triggers the chain of events resulting in myosin heads binding to actin.

q: What provides the energy for the power stroke?
e: ATP powers the myosin heads pulling actin toward the sarcomere centre. After the power stroke the myosin detach and return to resting length.

q: What is the primary purpose of small motor units?
o: Moving the body, as in running and jumping
Stabilising the body, as in upright posture
e: Small motor units are fatigue resistant, contain Type I fibres, produce small forces slowly and primarily stabilise. Large motor units contain Type II fibres and move the body.

q: What does the all-or-nothing principle state?
o: A muscle either contracts completely or tears under load
An action potential activates every fibre in the motor unit
Every motor unit in a muscle fires at the same time
Contraction strength depends only on the size of the muscle
e: A motor unit cannot grade its own force: all the way or not at all. Overall contraction strength therefore depends on which type of motor unit is recruited and how many are activated.

q: Which is true of Type I fibres?
o: Larger and white, with low oxidative capacity
Smaller and red, with more capillaries and mitochondria
Fast to produce tension and quick to fatigue
Larger, with fewer mitochondria but greater fatigue resistance
e: Type I are slow-twitch, red, richer in capillaries, mitochondria and myoglobin, with higher oxidative capacity and better fatigue resistance. Type II are fast-twitch, white and larger.

q: Why are Type I fibres red?
o: More blood vessels running across the surface
They store more glycogen than Type II
They contain more actin than myosin
e: Myoglobin sits in the sarcoplasm and is similar to haemoglobin, the red pigment of red blood cells. Type I fibres carry more of it, along with more capillaries and mitochondria.

q: After age 50, muscle mass is lost at an average rate of:
e: Peak mass, power and strength occur between 20 and 30, change little from 30 to 50, then decline by 1 to 2 percent a year. Resistance training is highly beneficial against this.

q: A muscle exerting less force than is placed on it, lengthening under control, is performing which action?
e: Eccentric action is synonymous with deceleration, and is often called the negative. Landing from a jump is eccentric.

q: Isometric action means:
o: The muscle shortens as it produces force
The muscle produces force with no change in length
The muscle lengthens under control while producing force
The muscle produces no force at all
e: Force equals load, so nothing moves. Also called dynamic stabilisation; the rotator cuff holding the shoulder during a push-up is the example.

q: Concentric action is synonymous with:
e: Concentric means exerting more force than is placed on the muscle, so it shortens. Eccentric is deceleration, isometric is dynamic stabilisation.

q: Why train the entire muscle-action spectrum rather than emphasising concentric work?
o: It shortens the time each session takes
It maximises strength and protects range of motion
It reduces the total training volume needed
It allows heavier loads on every exercise in the programme
e: Traditional routines emphasise concentric production alone. Adding eccentric and isometric work maximises strength potential, maintains joint range of motion and prevents injury.

q: A muscle's role as agonist, synergist, stabiliser or antagonist depends on:
o: The joint motion at that moment
The client's fitness level and training age
e: Roles switch. The infraspinatus is an agonist for shoulder external rotation, a synergist when the shoulder reaches overhead, and a stabiliser during other shoulder motions.

q: Which muscle is the agonist for hip extension?
e: Gluteus maximus is the prime mover for hip extension; the hamstrings act as synergist. The hip flexor complex is the antagonist.

q: In a squat, which muscle acts as the stabiliser in NASM's table?
e: Transversus abdominis stabilises the spine. In the same table the agonists are gluteus maximus and quadriceps, the synergist is the hamstrings and the antagonist is the psoas.

q: How does a stabiliser contract?
o: Concentrically, shortening as the movers work
Isometrically, holding the joint in place
e: Holding a joint in place means producing force without changing length. Examples are transversus abdominis in a squat or overhead press, and the rotator cuff in a push-up.

q: In a chest press, which muscle is the antagonist?
e: Pectoralis major is the agonist, anterior deltoid and triceps the synergists, rotator cuff the stabiliser, posterior deltoid the antagonist.

q: What is feed-forward activation?
o: Contracting harder as fatigue sets in during a set
Stabilising a joint by contracting before the movement
Recruiting the prime mover before the synergists in every lift
Pre-stretching a muscle to increase the force it can produce
e: The stabilising contraction comes before the movement rather than in response to it. It is one reason muscles work in nervous-system-controlled groups rather than in isolation.

q: In the body, what plays the role of the fulcrum?
e: The joint axis is the fulcrum, the bones are levers, the muscles create the effort, and the resistance is body weight or an external object.

q: A biceps curl is which class of lever?
o: First class, with the fulcrum in the middle
Second class, with the resistance in the middle
Third class, with the effort in the middle
Second class, with the effort in the middle
e: Elbow fulcrum, biceps effort, dumbbell resistance, so the effort sits in the middle. Most limbs are third class, and the effort must exceed the resistance because it travels the shorter distance.

q: A calf raise, with the ball of the foot as fulcrum, is which class of lever?
o: First, with the fulcrum between effort and load
Second, with the resistance in the middle
Third, with the effort in the middle
Third, with the fulcrum at the ankle
e: Second class puts the resistance in the middle, as in a wheelbarrow. A full-body push-up is the other example given; first class puts the fulcrum in the middle, as in nodding the head.

q: Muscles can only pull, never push. What follows for joint motion?
o: Joints are moved mainly by external forces acting on the limb
All joint motion comes from muscles pulling on bones
Antagonists push the bone back to its starting position
Tendons supply the pushing force the muscle cannot
e: The musculoskeletal system is a series of levers and pulleys, with bones as levers and joints as fulcrums. A muscle can only shorten toward its attachments, so every joint motion is a pull.

q: Which part of the neuron transmits impulses to other neurons or to effector sites?
e: The axon is the cylindrical projection carrying impulses out. Dendrites gather information from other structures; the cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and controls the cell.

q: What are the four primary electrolytes needed for proper nerve function?
e: Electrolytes are minerals carrying an electrical charge. Neurons signal both electrically and chemically.

q: A client walks from pavement onto sand and alters their walking pattern. In which order do the nervous system's three functions occur?
o: Sensory, then motor, with no integrative step
e: Sensory detects the change of surface, integrative analyses and interprets it, motor produces the neuromuscular response.

q: The peripheral nervous system consists of:
o: The brain and the spinal cord
12 cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves
31 cranial nerves and 12 pairs of spinal nerves
Interneurons within the spinal cord only
e: Twelve cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the sensory receptors. The brain and spinal cord are the CNS; interneurons exist only inside it.

q: Afferent pathways carry information:
o: Down from the CNS to the muscles
Up to the CNS; they are sensory
From one effector site to another, bypassing the CNS
Only between neurons inside the brain and spinal cord
e: Afferent is sensory and travels up; efferent is motor and travels down. Interneurons are the ones confined to the spinal cord and brain.

q: Which sensory receptor type relates most to the science of human movement?
e: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical forces, touch and pressure, making them the most important for a fitness professional. Nociceptors respond to pain, chemoreceptors to smell and taste, photoreceptors to light.

q: Muscle spindles run parallel to the muscle fibres and are sensitive to:
o: Muscular tension and its rate of change
Muscle length and the rate of length change
e: They regulate contraction through the stretch reflex mechanism, returning a contract response within 1 to 2 milliseconds to protect the muscle from stretching too far or too fast.

q: What happens when a Golgi tendon organ is activated?
e: GTOs sit where skeletal muscle fibres insert into the tendons and sense change in muscular tension and its rate. Activation causes the muscle to relax, preventing excessive stress and possible injury.

q: Joint receptors signal:
o: Change in muscle length and its rate of change
e: Joint receptors sit in and around the joint capsule and respond to pressure, acceleration and deceleration. Length is the muscle spindle's job, tension the Golgi tendon organ's, pain the nociceptors'.

q: Proprioception is:
o: The ability to feel pain and pressure
The sense of the body's position in space
The speed at which a nerve impulse travels
Conscious, voluntary control of skeletal muscle
e: Proprioception is the body's ability to sense its general orientation and the relative position of all its parts. Training it improves balance, coordination and posture without conscious thought.

q: Which division produces the fight-or-flight response?
e: Sympathetic increases neural activity, signals endocrine organs to release hormones such as adrenaline, and raises heart rate, breathing and alertness. Parasympathetic is rest and digest.

q: A client is just learning a skill and performance is inconsistent. Which stage is this, and what should the trainer do?
o: Associative; refine through practice and feedback
Cognitive; simple instructions and small steps
e: The three stages are cognitive, associative and autonomous. Associative gets practice and regular feedback; autonomous gets new versions to further challenge them.

q: Bioenergetics is:
o: The capacity of the body to do work
The study of energy conversion in the human body
The measurement of oxygen uptake during exercise testing
The sum of the three energy pathways combined
e: Bioenergetics studies how the chemical energy in food becomes mechanical energy. Energy itself is the capacity to do work.

q: Which side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood, and where does it pump it?
e: The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs. The left receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the entire body.

q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
o: It holds a greater volume of blood
It pumps at higher pressure to the whole body
It receives blood at higher pressure from the lungs
e: The right ventricle pumps only as far as the lungs and under low pressure, so its wall stays thin. The left has to drive blood around the entire body.

q: Which structure is the pacemaker of the heart?
o: The SA node in the right atrium
e: The SA node initiates the signal. Internodal pathways carry it to the AV node, which delays it so the ventricles can fill before contracting. The result is normal sinus rhythm.

q: Why does the AV node delay the impulse?
o: To slow the overall heart rate at rest and in exercise
To let the ventricles fill before contracting
To protect the myocardial cells from overload
To synchronise the heartbeat with breathing
e: Without the delay the ventricles would begin contracting before the atria had emptied into them. The pause is what makes proper filling possible.

q: Blood makes up approximately what proportion of total body weight?
e: About 8 percent, roughly 5 litres in the average person, and it is thicker and heavier than water.

q: Which blood cells contain growth factors that may help healing after injury?
e: Platelets assist with clotting and contain growth factors. Those factors assist vasculogenesis, the formation of new capillaries, and angiogenesis, formation of new capillaries from existing vessels.

q: Which vessels are the exchange sites of water and chemicals between blood and tissues?
e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries are the smallest vessels and the exchange sites.

q: In capillary exchange, which substances only exit into the tissues?
e: Water both enters and exits, carbon dioxide only enters from the tissues, and glucose and oxygen only exit into the tissues.

q: Which are the primary respiratory muscles used in quiet breathing?
e: Quiet inspiration uses the diaphragm and external intercostals. Heavy or forced breathing additionally recruits the secondary muscles: scalenes, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor.

q: In quiet breathing, expiration is:
o: Active, driven by the expiratory muscles compressing the chest
Passive, as the inspiratory muscles relax
e: Inspiration is always active: contracting the inspiratory muscles increases thoracic volume and drops intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric, drawing air in. Quiet expiration is passive.

q: Normal respiratory rate at rest is:
e: 12 to 16 at rest. Tachypnea is above 24, bradypnea below 8.

q: Where does gas exchange with the bloodstream take place?
e: Alveoli sit in clusters of alveolar sacs at the end of the bronchioles, surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses across the capillary membranes into the blood.

q: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the heart through the:
o: Pulmonary arteries, into the right atrium
Pulmonary veins, into the left atrium
Vena cava, into the right ventricle
e: Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries; oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, then out to the tissues.

q: The conducting airways do more than carry air. What else do they do?
o: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood
Purify, humidify and warm or cool the air
Trap and store carbon dioxide before exhalation
Regulate the rate and depth of breathing
e: The nasal and oral cavities, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchioles condition the air to body temperature as they carry it. Gas exchange happens further on, in the alveoli.

q: Efficient oxygen uptake depends on three things. Which is NOT one of them?
o: The respiratory system's ability to collect oxygen
The cardiovascular system's ability to absorb and transport it
The tissues' ability to use it
The kidneys' ability to filter it
e: The three are collection by the respiratory system, absorption and transport by the cardiovascular system, and use by the tissues. The kidneys play no part in oxygen uptake.

q: Aside from surgery, how is mass physically removed from the body?
o: Through urine and other fluid losses
Through heat radiated from the skin
e: We are carbon-based, so exhaled carbon dioxide is the route out. Related point: fat cannot be burned without the presence of oxygen.

q: A client shows a rapid shallow upper-chest breathing pattern. What should you do?
o: Correct it with breathing drills, since it is a movement fault
Ignore it, since breathing is entirely outside a trainer's scope
Stop training the client until a physician clears them
e: An abnormal breathing pattern is a medical matter and warrants referral, but teaching correct breathing stays within scope. Consequences of the pattern include dizziness, anxiety, fatigue, poor sleep and poor circulation.

q: Which two energy pathways are anaerobic?
e: ATP-PCr and glycolysis do not require oxygen. The oxidative pathway is aerobic. Together the three form the bioenergetic continuum.

q: Which system is activated at the onset of any activity, regardless of intensity?
o: Whichever system matches the intensity of the activity
e: ATP-PCr produces energy fastest, so it covers the first seconds of anything, then sustains only about 10 seconds before another system takes over.

q: How much energy does the creatine phosphate reaction release for muscle contraction?
e: Creatine phosphate plus ADP yields creatine plus ATP, releasing 7.3 kcals. ATP and PCr are phosphagens, hence the alternative name, the phosphagen system.

q: At what intensity does the ATP-PCr system predominate?
e: 90 to 100 percent: power and strength training with heavy loads and few repetitions, or short sprinting.

q: How many ATP does one glucose molecule produce through anaerobic glycolysis?
e: Two ATP, with pyruvate as a by-product. If the cell cannot use pyruvate fast enough, lactic acid builds up, increasing cell acidity, interfering with contraction and decreasing performance.

q: A typical set of 8 to 12 repetitions primarily stresses which system?
e: Glycolysis covers moderate to high intensity for roughly 30 to 60 seconds, and a typical 8 to 12 rep range falls inside that window.

q: What distinguishes fast glycolysis from slow glycolysis?
o: Fast is aerobic and slow is anaerobic
Fast is anaerobic; slow is aerobic and slower
Fast uses fat as its substrate, slow uses carbohydrate
Fast produces more ATP per glucose molecule than slow does
e: Both break down glucose; the difference is oxygen. Fast glycolysis runs at 80 to 90 percent intensity for about one to two minutes, and intensity has to come down to run the aerobic version.

q: How many ATP does one glucose molecule yield through the oxidative system?
e: Thirty-six, and up to 38 depending on substrates and pathways. With oxygen present, pyruvate is not converted to lactic acid and instead becomes a substrate for further ATP production.

q: Why is the oxidative system the slowest to produce energy?
o: It relies on fat, which is slow to break down into fuel
Elevating respiration to match demand takes time
It produces the least ATP of the three systems
It only operates fully when the body is at rest
e: The system needs oxygen in amounts matching the muscular requirement, and raising respiration to supply it takes time. It is the slowest but produces the most, predominating beyond 2 minutes.

q: Fat, carbohydrate and protein enter the oxidative system by different routes. Where do they converge?
e: Fat becomes free fatty acids then beta-oxidation; carbohydrate becomes glucose then glycolysis then pyruvate; protein becomes amino acids then deamination. All converge on acetyl-CoA, then the citric acid cycle, then the electron transport chain.

q: At lower intensity levels there is a primary reliance on:
e: The oxidative system draws primarily on carbohydrate and fat, and at low intensity the primary reliance is on fat. It also covers standing, sitting and working, making it the system behind most of daily life.

q: What is the relationship between intensity and duration?
o: Inverse: as intensity rises, duration falls
It depends on the client's fitness and training age
e: Intensity and duration have an inverse relationship. That, plus the fact that all three systems keep working while one predominates, are the two governing principles.

q: When one energy system is predominant, what are the others doing?
o: Still working, recovering for their next turn
Being actively inhibited by the nervous system
e: The non-dominant systems are not supplying most of the energy, but they stay active and recover ready for their next turn.

q: Which training approach best develops the glycolytic system?
o: Interval training with short recovery periods
Short-duration high-intensity work with long rests
e: ATP-PCr wants short high-intensity work with adequate rest for phosphocreatine recovery. Oxidative wants long-duration moderate-intensity work. Glycolysis wants intervals with short recoveries.

q: What does FITTE-VP stand for?
o: Frequency, intensity, time, type, enjoyment, volume, progression
Frequency, intensity, tempo, training, endurance, velocity, power
Fitness, intensity, time, technique, effort, volume, periodisation
Frequency, interval, time, type, exertion, variety, progression
e: Frequency, intensity, time, type, enjoyment, volume and progression. Enjoyment is in there because a programme the client abandons has no effect.

q: In the FITTE-VP principle, what does the 'V' stand for?
e: Volume, the total amount of work performed.

q: How is intensity defined?
o: The speed at which an exercise is performed
The level of demand that a given activity places on the body
The total work completed in a session
The percentage of maximal heart rate reached
e: Intensity is the level of demand a given activity places on the body. It can be monitored several ways, but the definition is about demand, not any one measurement.

q: What does the principle of progression in cardiorespiratory training involve?
o: Gradually increasing exercise intensity, duration or frequency
Maintaining the same routine for consistency
Reducing workout duration as fitness improves
e: Progression means gradually increasing intensity, duration or frequency. In stage training it is capped at no more than 10% added volume per week.

q: How often should moderate-intensity exercise such as brisk walking be performed?
e: Moderate intensity at least 5 times per week, vigorous intensity at least 3 times per week. A combination of the two also works.

q: Which formula does NASM prefer for estimating maximal heart rate?
o: 200 minus age plus resting heart rate
e: The Tanaka formula, 208 minus 0.7 times age. It is more accurate than the traditional 220 minus age.

q: What is the main problem with the 220 minus age formula?
o: It underestimates maximal heart rate in everyone
It was never intended for designing cardio fitness programmes
It requires a maximal effort test to validate
It only applies to trained athletes
e: Haskell's formula, 220 minus age, was never intended as an instrument for designing programmes, because maximal heart rate varies significantly between individuals of the same age.

q: Why is heart rate reserve, the Karvonen method, considered more appropriate than using a percentage of maximal heart rate alone?
o: It is easier to calculate in the gym
It accounts for the individual's resting heart rate
It does not require knowing the client's age
It produces a higher target heart rate
e: Heart rate reserve works from the difference between estimated maximum and resting heart rate, so it accounts for resting heart rate, which varies between people and reflects conditioning.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the methods given for monitoring cardiorespiratory exercise intensity?
e: The six methods are VO2max, percentage of maximal heart rate, percentage of heart rate reserve, METs, RPE and the talk test. Percentage of 1RM is a resistance training variable.

q: Why is direct VO2max measurement impractical for most fitness professionals?
o: The equipment is illegal outside a hospital
It requires the client to exercise at maximal effort under ventilation monitoring
It can only be performed on a treadmill
It takes several days to produce a result
e: It requires a maximal effort while sophisticated equipment monitors the ventilation response, so submaximal tests are used to estimate VO2max instead.

q: What percentage of maximal heart rate is recommended for a beginner?
e: Beginners 65 to 75%, intermediate 80 to 85%, advanced up to 90%. Do not confuse this with the zone table, where zone 1 is 50 to 60%.

q: What marks the first ventilatory threshold, VT1?
o: The point where the client can no longer speak at all
The point where continuous conversation stops being effortless
The point where heart rate reaches 75% of maximum
e: VT1 is where breathing starts rising disproportionately and continuous conversation becomes challenging. VT2 is higher, where speech drops to short phrases.

q: Which training zone sits above VT2?
e: Zone 1 is below VT1, zone 2 runs VT1 to the midpoint, zone 3 the midpoint to VT2, and zone 4 is above VT2, where speech is impossible or limited to single words.

q: In the training zone table, what is the 'midpoint'?
o: The intensity halfway between VT1 and VT2
The middle of the session by duration
e: The midpoint is the intensity level halfway between the two ventilatory thresholds, and it separates zone 2 from zone 3.

q: What is the talk test actually doing?
o: Providing a rough substitute when no other method is available
Locating the ventilatory thresholds without laboratory gas analysis
Assessing the client's motivation to continue
e: It is the field method for finding VT1 and VT2 without a metabolic cart, which is why every training zone is described by what speech is still possible.

q: What is the purpose of a warm-up in cardiorespiratory training?
o: To prepare the body for more intense exercise by gradually increasing heart rate and blood flow
e: The warm-up gradually raises heart rate and blood flow to prepare for harder work. Warm-up and cool-down are the two components most often skipped.

q: Which of these is an example of aerobic exercise?
e: Cycling is sustained activity using oxygen for energy. Sprinting, weightlifting and HIIT are anaerobic, relying on short bursts of high-intensity work.

q: What is a key characteristic of aerobic exercise?
o: Sustained activity using oxygen for energy
Immediate energy drawn from creatine phosphate
e: Aerobic means with oxygen, so the defining feature is sustained activity fuelled oxidatively.

q: Which training zones does Stage 1 use?
e: Stage 1 is low-intensity steady-state work below VT1, which is zone 1 only. It is the only stage that maps to a single zone.

q: What is the criterion for moving a client from Stage 1 to Stage 2?
o: Holding zone 1 intensity for 30 minutes, three times per week
e: The gate is zone 1 for 30 minutes three times a week. A deconditioned client may need two to three months to get there.

q: What must be recorded before Stage 3 intervals can be programmed?
o: Resting blood pressure and body fat percentage
One-repetition maximum for the main lifts
e: Stage 3 moves between zones 1, 2 and 3, and the zone boundaries are defined by the ventilatory thresholds, so both must be measured.

q: Stage 3 is described as NOT appropriate for which clients?
o: Those seeking modest improvements, those new to exercise, and those averse to high-intensity training
Clients training fewer than five days per week
Clients whose primary goal is weight loss
e: The course names those three groups explicitly. People wanting modest gains do not need to move on to Stage 3 at all.

q: Who is Stage 4 reserved for?
o: Any client who has completed Stage 3
e: Stage 4 raises anaerobic capacity above VT2 and is reserved for athletes and top-end fitness competitors. Like Stage 3 it requires VT1 and VT2 recorded.

q: In the example Stage 2 interval workout, what is the work-to-recovery structure?
o: 1 minute in zone 2 against 3 minutes of zone 1 recovery
5 minutes in zone 2 against 1 minute of zone 1 recovery
2 minutes in zone 3 against 2 minutes of zone 1 recovery
Continuous zone 2 with no recovery periods
e: After a 5 to 10 minute zone 1 warm-up, 1 minute of zone 2 work alternates with 3 minutes of zone 1 recovery.

q: How does a client progress within Stage 2 before total volume is increased?
o: By adding a fourth training day
By tightening the work-to-rest ratio from 1:3 to 1:2 to 1:1
By moving some intervals into zone 3
e: Work-to-rest ratios of 1:3, 1:2 and 1:1 adjust as the client progresses. Workload within the intervals is raised through speed and incline.

q: What limits how quickly training volume should rise?
o: No more than 10% added volume per week
No more than 25% added volume per week
Volume should double every four weeks
e: Exceeding 10% added volume per week risks overtraining and burnout.

q: For a client new to interval training, what is the recommended approach when introducing Stage 2?
o: Convert every session to Stage 2 at once
Alternate Stage 1 and Stage 2 workouts, rotating which stage starts the week
Drop to two sessions per week until adapted
e: Alternating means Stage 1 Monday, Stage 2 Wednesday, Stage 1 Friday, then starting the next week with Stage 2. Most of the total time still sits in zone 1.

q: Which stage of cardiorespiratory training focuses on increasing intensity and duration to maximise performance?
e: Stage 3 is for the moderately advanced client and raises both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, moving between zones 1, 2 and 3. Stage 4 is a narrower case reserved for athletes.

q: How should a hard Stage 3 training day be followed?
o: With a second Stage 3 day to consolidate
e: Rotate all three stages and use a Stage 1 day as a recovery day after a hard Stage 3 day.

q: What factor most significantly influences poor flexibility?
e: Modern sedentary life produces predictable patterns of movement impairment, which is why clients present with similar assessment findings.

q: What is the correct order of the corrective exercise continuum?
e: Inhibit the overactive tissue, lengthen it, activate the underactive muscle, then integrate the result into whole movement.

q: Which technique corresponds to the 'inhibit' step of the corrective exercise continuum?
e: Inhibit uses self-myofascial release, lengthen uses static stretching, activate uses isolated strengthening and integrate uses dynamic movement.

q: Which technique involves the use of foam rolling?
e: Self-myofascial release applies sustained pressure to release tension, most commonly with a foam roller.

q: What is the recommended duration for a self-myofascial release repetition?
e: The acute variables table gives daily frequency, one set, 20 to 30 seconds per spot. Other figures appear across the course, but answer from the table.

q: What are the acute variables for static stretching?
o: 1 to 3 repetitions, held 30 seconds each, daily
3 to 5 repetitions, held 10 seconds each, twice weekly
5 repetitions, held 15 seconds each, three times weekly
e: Daily, 1 to 3 repetitions, holding each stretch for 30 seconds.

q: What are the acute variables for dynamic stretching?
e: One set of 10 repetitions across 3 to 10 exercises.

q: How is static stretching defined?
o: Actively contracting the opposing muscle to lengthen the target
Passively taking a muscle to the point of tension and holding it
Moving a joint repeatedly through its range at speed
Applying sustained pressure to a tender point
e: Passively taking the muscle to the point of tension and holding it for a minimum of 20 to 30 seconds.

q: How is dynamic stretching defined?
o: Holding a lengthened position while breathing deeply
Using the force production of a muscle and the body's momentum to take a joint through its full available range
Having a partner apply pressure at end range
Rolling a muscle until the tension dissipates
e: It uses the muscle's own force production plus momentum, and the movements mimic the higher-intensity activity that follows.

q: What is the primary benefit of static stretching?
o: Improving tissue extensibility and joint range of motion
e: Static stretching improves tissue extensibility and range of motion, and resets muscles to their proper length-tension relationships.

q: What is the primary benefit of dynamic stretching?
o: Increasing tissue temperature and heart rate
e: Dynamic stretching raises tissue temperature, heart rate and respiration, and improves the nervous system's ability to contract muscles forcefully.

q: What is a contraindication for dynamic stretching?
e: Dynamic stretching is an advanced technique. Poor tissue extensibility, poor posture, poor core strength and poor balance all contraindicate it.

q: If a client has muscle imbalances, what should precede dynamic stretching?
o: Self-myofascial release and static stretching for the overactive muscles
e: Release and lengthen the overactive muscles identified in the movement assessment first. Where no imbalances exist, go straight to dynamic work.

q: What does the word yoga mean?
e: Yoga is Sanskrit for yoke or union, referring to the union of mind and body.

q: What is the main focus of yoga in a Western context?
o: Physical postures, and improving flexibility and strength
e: What the West calls yoga is technically Hatha yoga, focused on the physical postures or asanas, combined with breathing.

q: Why should a stretching session never cause pain?
o: It makes the client less likely to return
Pain shifts the client into the sympathetic nervous system, the opposite of what the session needs
e: Pain turns a relaxing session into a tension-filled one, moving the client into fight or flight under sympathetic control.

q: What is the core defined as in core training?
o: The muscles of the arms and legs
The structures making up the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex, including the lumbar spine, pelvic girdle, abdomen and hip joint
The chest and upper back muscles
e: The core is the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex, not the abdominals alone.

q: Which muscle belongs to the core movement system?
e: Rectus abdominis crosses joints and produces motion. Transverse abdominis, pelvic floor and multifidus are all stabilisation system muscles.

q: Which muscle is the flagship of the core stabilization system?
e: Transverse abdominis runs horizontally and compresses rather than moves the spine. It is the muscle the drawing-in manoeuvre exists to recruit.

q: What is a primary function of the stabilization system in the core?
e: The stabilisation system holds the spine and pelvis in position. Producing trunk movement is the movement system's job.

q: What is the drawing-in manoeuvre used for?
o: Recruiting the local core stabilisers by drawing the navel toward the spine
e: It draws the navel toward the spine and holds that position to activate the local stabilisers.

q: During the drawing-in manoeuvre, what indicates improper activation?
e: There should be no movement of the extremities. Movement indicates the larger movement muscles are compensating.

q: What should a core training programme initially focus on?
e: Stabilisation comes first and builds the foundation, with a progression gate of one to two months before core strength work.

q: Which exercise is an example of a core stabilization exercise?
e: The floor bridge produces little to no movement of the spine and pelvis. Ball crunches and cable rotations are strength exercises and the pullover throw is power.

q: What type of core exercise involves dynamic eccentric and concentric movements of the spine?
e: Core strength work moves the spine dynamically through eccentric and concentric phases, unlike stabilisation work which holds position.

q: What is the main purpose of core power exercises?
o: Increasing the rate of force production
e: Core power raises the rate of force production, which is speed and power, preparing the body for high-intensity sport-specific action.

q: Which exercise belongs to the core power level?
e: Throws are power exercises. Marching and the plank are stabilisation, and back extension is strength.

q: What is one benefit of core training?
e: Core training improves dynamic postural control, which is the ability to hold position while moving.

q: Why is a neutral cervical spine position important during core training?
o: It increases flexibility of the neck muscles
It helps avoid exercise-induced injury by reducing compressive forces on the cervical spine
e: Neutral cervical position keeps compressive load off the neck during core work.

q: What should be avoided to prevent compressive forces on the cervical spine during core exercises?
o: Moving the head from side to side
Allowing the head to fall forward
e: The head falling forward is the deviation that loads the cervical spine. Stretching the neck is not a compressive-loading issue.

q: What is the benefit of training the core movement system after stabilization has been developed?
o: It ensures optimal force production, reduction and stabilization of the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex
e: With stabilisation established, the movement system can produce, reduce and stabilise force through the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex.

q: What is the principle of adaptation in resistance training?
o: The body adjusts to the demands placed on it through repeated exposure
e: Adaptation means the body adjusts to imposed demands, which is why the stressor has to be met repeatedly for change to occur.

q: What are the three stages of the General Adaptation Syndrome?
o: Alarm phase, resistance development stage, exhaustion stage
Initial phase, training phase, rest phase
e: Alarm, resistance development and exhaustion. There is no fourth stage, so any option offering a recovery phase is wrong.

q: What happens during the alarm phase of the General Adaptation Syndrome?
o: The body reaches a plateau in performance
Performance significantly improves due to adaptation
The body experiences tiredness, tightness or muscle pain
The body recovers and returns to homeostasis
e: Alarm is the initial disruption, producing tiredness, tightness or delayed-onset soreness 6 to 48 hours after unfamiliar exercise.

q: Which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome involves adaptation and improved performance?
e: Resistance development is where physiological adaptation happens and performance improves. If a question mentions improved performance, this is the stage.

q: How long after unfamiliar exercise does the alarm phase typically appear?
o: Immediately and only during the session
e: Soreness appears 6 to 48 hours afterwards. It signals muscle injury but not how severe that injury is.

q: What is the SAID principle in resistance training?
o: Specific aerobic improvements due to diet
Specific anaerobic increases due to exercise
e: Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands, also called the principle of specificity. The body adapts to the type of exercise performed.

q: What does mechanical specificity refer to?
o: The weight and movements used in training
The energy systems targeted during exercise
The type of recovery techniques used
e: Mechanical specificity is the weight and movements used. Neuromuscular specificity is speed and control, and metabolic specificity is the energy systems targeted.

q: What does neuromuscular specificity refer to?
o: The weight lifted in each set
The speed and control with which an exercise is performed
The number of muscle groups involved
e: Stability exercises performed slowly improve control, while high-velocity movements build power. That is neuromuscular specificity.

q: What is the principle of overload?
o: Training to failure on every set
Increasing the intensity or volume of exercise using a systematic and gradual approach
Lifting the heaviest possible load each session
Adding a new exercise every week
e: Overload means increasing intensity or volume systematically and gradually. There are more ways to make an exercise harder than adding weight.

q: How is strength defined?
o: The size of a muscle's cross-section
The ability of the neuromuscular system to provide internal tension and exert force against external resistance
The speed at which a muscle can contract
The length of time a contraction can be held
e: Strength is a neuromuscular property, not just a muscular one, which is why early gains appear before any visible growth.

q: Why do beginners often gain strength rapidly with no visible increase in muscle size?
o: Their muscles grow internally without changing shape
The nervous system improves at recruiting muscle fibres
Connective tissue thickens before muscle does
They lose fat at the same rate muscle is gained
e: Early strength gains are neural. The higher the stimulus, the more fibres are recruited, and the more fibres contract the more resistance can be overcome.

q: What is a force-couple relationship?
o: The balance between agonist and antagonist muscles
The relationship between muscle length and tension
The synergistic action of multiple muscles working together to produce movement around a joint
The adaptation of muscles to different resistance levels
e: Muscles are recruited in groups, each pulling on bone from a different attachment and angle, and the resulting motion depends on their collective pull.

q: What are the suggested acute variables for stabilization and muscular endurance training?
o: 12 to 20 or more reps, 1 to 3 sets, 50 to 70% 1RM
1 to 10 reps, 3 to 6 sets, light load
e: Moderate to high repetitions, low to moderate sets, low to moderate intensity.

q: What are the suggested acute variables for maximal strength training?
o: 8 to 10 reps, 3 to 5 sets, light load
e: Low repetitions, high sets, high training intensities.

q: What load is used for power training, and why?
o: Heavy, because force production is the goal
Light, because the emphasis is on speed
Moderate, to balance force and velocity
