e: Light loads, around 10% of body weight with a medicine ball or 30 to 45% with weights, because velocity is the training variable.

q: In NASM's tempo notation, what order are the three numbers given in?
e: Eccentric first, then isometric, then concentric. So 4/2/1 is a four-second lowering, a two-second hold and a one-second lift.

q: Why is the eccentric phase the longest in the recommended starting tempo?
o: It is the easiest phase to control
Most injuries occur during the deceleration phase
It produces the most muscle soreness
e: Most injuries happen during deceleration, so the eccentric is emphasised early at 2 to 4 seconds against 1 to 2 for the other phases.

q: In which plane of motion do most injuries occur?
e: Most injuries occur during rotational movement, which is why an integrated programme must train all three planes.

q: Which type of resistance equipment is most beneficial for improving core and postural stability?
e: Free weights require the stabiliser muscles to work. Machines provide artificial support and do little to challenge the core stabilisation system.

q: What is a main disadvantage of weight machines?
o: They do little to challenge the core stabilization system
They cannot provide enough load for strength training
e: Machines move in one plane, offer artificial support, do little for core or dynamic joint stabilisation, and do not fit all body types.

q: What is a main advantage of elastic resistance bands?
o: They are portable and can be used anywhere
They provide consistent resistance throughout the movement
e: Portability and versatility. Resistance is in fact inconsistent through the range, and bands are not ideal for maximal strength.

q: Why is elastic resistance unsuitable for maximal strength training?
o: The bands break under heavy tension
High intensity requires heavy load, which bands cannot reliably provide
It cannot be used in a standing position
It only works for upper body exercises
e: Maximal strength needs high intensity. Band tension is also hard to quantify and varies between brands and with wear.

q: Why is body-weight training limited for developing maximal strength?
o: Body weight fluctuates very little, so heavier loads are unavailable
It cannot be progressed at all
It works only one plane of motion
e: Since body weight changes little, the load cannot be raised. Body-weight work can be regressed or progressed by varying speed or amplitude.

q: How many kinetic-chain checkpoints are there, and what are they?
o: Four: feet, knees, hips and head
Five: feet, knees, hips and low back, shoulders, head
Six: feet, ankles, knees, hips, shoulders, head
e: Feet, knees, hips and low back, shoulders, and head. They are the form standard and the screening tool for exercise selection.

q: Where should the knees point during a loaded movement?
o: Slightly inward, to engage the adductors
Straight ahead over the second and third toes
Outward beyond the line of the foot
Wherever feels natural to the client
e: Pointing the knees over the second and third toes prevents inward migration and reduces abnormal knee stress, mitigating ACL injury risk.

q: What is the correct breathing pattern during resistance training?
o: Inhale during the lifting phase, exhale during the lowering phase
Exhale during the most strenuous phase, the concentric or lifting portion
Hold the breath through the whole repetition for stability
Breathe only through the nose throughout
e: Exhale upon exertion. Inhale during the less strenuous phase, and above all keep breathing.

q: What does proper breathing during resistance training help to prevent?
o: Holding the breath during exertion, which can lead to dizziness or fainting
e: Breath-holding against a closed glottis spikes blood pressure and drops cerebral perfusion on release. It is singled out as especially important for clients with hypertension or heart conditions.

q: What is the primary benefit of proper posture during strength training?
o: Reducing unwanted stress on the spine and joints
e: Good posture ensures the correct muscles work the right way and joints are not excessively stressed.

q: What is the common myth about women and resistance training?
o: Women will develop large, bulky muscles like men
Women cannot gain strength from resistance training
Women should not lift heavy weights
Women do not need resistance training
e: Hormonal differences prevent the same degree of hypertrophy. Physiological responses to training are otherwise similar, and women can use the same exercises and techniques.

q: How does strength training aid weight loss?
o: It increases muscle mass, raising metabolic rate
e: Increased muscle mass slightly raises metabolic rate, the session itself costs calories, and metabolism stays elevated afterwards.

q: What is one benefit of strength training for general health?
e: Resistance training improves bone density and decreases osteoporosis risk. It also lowers resting heart rate and blood pressure over time.

q: What is the main purpose of strength training for athletes?
o: Enhancing force production, power and dynamic postural control
e: More force production means jumping higher, running faster and throwing further, with better dynamic postural control in all planes.

q: What is the primary focus of periodization in resistance training?
o: Strategically varying training variables over time
e: Periodization is the planned variation of training variables, which prevents plateaus and promotes continuous improvement.

q: Why is periodization important in resistance training programmes?
o: It eliminates the need for recovery periods
It increases the risk of injury
It prevents plateaus and promotes continuous improvement
It ensures exercises are performed at maximum intensity all the time
e: Varying the training variables prevents accommodation and keeps progress going, while also managing stress and providing planned recovery.

q: Which progression unit belongs to cardiorespiratory training rather than resistance training?
e: Cardio progresses through stages, resistance through phases. Zones belong to cardio only, and a set of squats does not have a zone.

q: How is resistance training intensity described, as opposed to cardio intensity?
o: By acute variables such as load, sets, reps and tempo
e: Zones are cardiorespiratory markers based on ventilatory thresholds. Resistance intensity is described by acute variables.

q: What is the primary objective of the stabilization phase in a resistance programme?
o: Develop foundational stability and improve joint stability
e: Stabilisation builds joint stability and muscular endurance, preparing the body for heavier lifting. It is about joints, not muscle size or the heart.

q: How is a strength exercise converted into a stability exercise?
o: By making the base of support less stable, such as using a ball or a single-leg stance
By increasing the number of repetitions only
e: Use a stability ball instead of a bench, or perform the exercise standing or on one leg. The environment must be unstable but controllable.

q: Why should heavy loads be lifted in stable environments rather than on balance devices?
o: Balance devices are too expensive for heavy loading
An unstable surface reduces force output, giving less force for more risk
Balance devices only suit upper body work
Machines are always safer than free weights
e: Unstable surfaces measurably reduce force production, so loading heavily on one is the worst of both. Balance devices should not be used for maximal or near-maximal lifts.

q: What is eustress?
o: Negative stress under which health and performance deteriorate
Positive stress under which health and performance continue to improve
Stress caused only by physical exertion
e: Eustress is positive stress, and resistance exercise is an example. Distress is where health and performance decline.

q: How does the body respond during the alarm-reaction stage of stress?
o: It decreases heart rate and blood flow
e: Alarm is activation, not settling. Anything describing the body calming down is wrong for this stage.

q: Which gland releases catecholamines during the fight-or-flight response, and what triggers it?
o: The thyroid, triggered by the pituitary
The adrenal glands, triggered by the hypothalamus
The pancreas, triggered by the liver
The pituitary, triggered by the adrenal glands
e: The hypothalamus signals the adrenal glands to release catecholamines, which raise heart rate, respiration and blood pressure, dilate pupils and release stored glucose.

q: Which technique is classified as a muscle-to-mind relaxation technique?
e: Muscle-to-mind has only three members: progressive muscle relaxation, massage and biofeedback. The other three options are all mind-to-muscle.

q: Which of these is a mind-to-muscle relaxation technique?
e: Mind-to-muscle covers yoga, meditation, visual imagery and autogenic training.

q: What is progressive muscle relaxation?
o: A massage sequence working from the feet upward
Deliberately tensing a muscle group, then releasing it and noticing the relaxation
Visualising each muscle relaxing in turn
Holding a stretch until the tension dissipates
e: A two-step process that teaches you to distinguish a tensed muscle from a relaxed one, so relaxation can be induced at the first sign of tension.

q: What is biofeedback?
o: Feedback given verbally by the trainer after each set
A technique using a machine to monitor biometrics such as heart rate, temperature and blood pressure
The body's internal signalling during exercise
A method of testing muscular endurance
e: Sensors give real-time information on normally involuntary processes, so the individual can learn to influence their autonomic nervous system.

q: What is one of the primary benefits of regular exercise in stress management?
o: It promotes the release of endorphins
It increases the amount of stress hormones
e: Exercise promotes endorphin release, reduces the adrenal hormones released in response to stress, and lowers resting blood pressure over time.

q: What are the three components of recovery?
e: Rest covers sleep above all, refuel covers hydration and nutrition, and regeneration means taking stress out of the body.

q: What does the course say about the optimal number of hours of sleep?
o: Exactly eight hours for every adult
There is no magic number, sleep is individualised
Six hours is sufficient for most people
Ten hours for anyone training regularly
e: Eight hours works as a practical shorthand with clients, but the research gives no magic number. Quality matters as well as quantity.

q: What is the importance of recovery in a resistance training programme?
o: Allowing the body to repair and strengthen muscles
e: Recovery lets the body repair and strengthen muscle, adapt to training stress, and avoid overtraining and injury.

q: How many levels and phases does the OPT model contain?
e: Three levels — stabilization, strength, power — containing five phases. Stabilization holds phase 1; strength holds phases 2, 3 and 4; power holds phase 5 alone.

q: All of the following phases make up the strength level of the OPT model except:
e: The strength level is phases 2, 3 and 4. Power is phase 5 and is its own level.

q: What is the repetition range in the stabilization endurance phase?
e: Phase 1 uses 12-20 repetitions at 50-70% of 1RM, 1-3 sets, slow 4/2/1 tempo, 0-90 seconds rest.

q: A deconditioned client needs connective tissue preparation and postural control. Which phase?
e: Phase 1, Stabilization Endurance. It is the answer whenever a question describes stability, endurance, connective tissue preparation or return from inactivity.

q: What are the acute variables for phase 4, Maximal Strength?
e: Phase 4 is 1-5 repetitions, 4-6 sets, 85-100% of 1RM, explosive X/X/X tempo, 3-5 minutes rest.

q: In the tempo notation 4/2/1, what does the 4 represent?
e: Tempo is written eccentric/isometric/concentric. 4/2/1 is a four-second lowering, two-second pause, one-second lift.

q: Which training levels use total body exercises?
e: Total body exercises are used at all three levels.

q: Phase 2, Strength Endurance, supersets a strength exercise with what?
e: Phase 2 pairs a strength exercise with a stabilization exercise. Phase 5 pairs strength with power.

q: Which of the following is a balance-stabilization exercise?
e: Balance-stabilization holds a position while something else moves: single-leg balance, balance reach, hip rotation, lift and chop, throw and catch.

q: All of the following are balance-stabilization exercises except:
e: The single-leg squat is balance-STRENGTH. It moves through a full range of motion rather than holding a position. This is the commonest trap in the topic.

q: Which is a balance-power exercise?
o: Multiplanar single-leg box hop-down with stabilization
e: Balance-power involves a hop and a landing, in multiple planes.

q: Balance is influenced by all of the following except:
e: NASM lists age, inactivity and injury as influences on balance. Bodyweight is not one of them.

q: How does balance training develop neuromuscular efficiency?
o: By simulating unstable yet controllable environments
By increasing joint range of motion
e: Balance training works by placing the body in unstable but controllable environments so the nervous system learns to stabilise.

q: All of the following are acute variables for balance-stabilization training except:
e: Sets, repetitions, tempo and rest are the acute variables for balance work. Intensity as a percentage of 1RM is not prescribed.

q: Which pairing reflects a correct stabilization progression?
e: The proprioceptive progression runs floor, balance beam, half foam roll, foam pad, balance disc, BOSU ball — progressively less stable.

q: Which of the following is an example of a core-stabilization exercise?
e: Core-stabilization uses little or no motion in the spine and pelvis: marching, floor bridge, floor prone cobra, plank.

q: What should be the focus in core-strength exercises?
o: Little to no motion in the spine
Dynamic movement of the spine through a full range of motion
e: Core-strength moves the spine dynamically through full range. Stabilization minimises spinal motion; power is explosive.

q: Which is the most progressive core training exercise?
e: Core-power is the most progressive stage, and the medicine ball throw is its signature exercise.

q: Which of the following is a common form mistake during a floor bridge?
o: Raising hips too far off the floor
e: Raising the hips too high extends the lumbar spine instead of extending the hips.

q: During the reverse crunch, which of the following is a common form mistake?
e: Swinging the legs uses momentum instead of the abdominals.

q: Which of the following is a concern during the ball crunch exercise?
o: Tilting the chin up toward the ceiling
Breathing out on the way up
e: Tilting the chin up puts the cervical spine into extension. The chin should stay tucked.

q: Which of the following is a common form mistake during the floor prone cobra?
e: Hyperextending the low back shifts the work from the scapular retractors to the lumbar extensors.

q: Which is a plyometric-stabilization exercise?
e: Plyometric-stabilization holds the landing for 3 to 5 seconds. Strength repeats without holding; power is as fast as controllable.

q: How long is the landing held in plyometric-stabilization exercises?
e: Three to five seconds, which is what makes it the stabilization stage.

q: In pronation distortion syndrome, all of the following are shortened muscles except:
e: The anterior tibialis is lengthened and underactive in pronation distortion syndrome, not shortened.

q: In upper crossed syndrome, all of the following are overactive in the head and neck except:
e: The deep cervical flexors are underactive and lengthened in upper crossed syndrome.

q: In upper crossed syndrome, which altered joint mechanic is present?
e: Upper crossed presents as forward head, rounded shoulders, increased thoracic kyphosis and increased scapular protraction and elevation.

q: Lower crossed syndrome typically presents with which pelvic position?
e: Anterior pelvic tilt with increased lumbar extension, from overactive hip flexors and erector spinae against underactive glutes and abdominals.

q: Which muscle group is underactive in lower crossed syndrome?
e: The gluteus maximus and medius, transverse abdominis and internal oblique are underactive. Hip flexors, erector spinae and latissimus dorsi are overactive.

q: Pronation distortion syndrome presents with which knee position?
e: Knee valgus — adduction and internal rotation — along with foot pronation and ankle eversion.

q: For effective weight loss, how many calories should an obese client expend per session?
e: NASM gives 200 to 300 calories expended per session.

q: How long should a client with coronary heart disease be asymptomatic before resistance training?
e: At least three months asymptomatic.

q: For older adults, what is the recommended resistance training intensity?
e: 40 to 80% of 1RM. Older adults achieve real improvements in muscular fitness through resistance training.

q: What assessments are appropriate for a client with hypertension?
e: The talk test avoids the maximal effort and the Valsalva response that raise risk in hypertension.

q: What resistance prescription suits an initial programme for a client with high blood pressure?
e: 1 to 3 sets of 10 to 20 repetitions — lower load, higher repetitions, avoiding maximal effort.

q: All of the following are skinfold sites used in the Durnin formula except:
e: The Durnin formula uses four sites: biceps, triceps, subscapular and suprailiac. Midaxillary belongs to the seven-site formula.

q: Which assessments best suit advanced clients such as athletes?
o: Bench press, squat, Shark Skill and Davies
e: Bench press and squat for upper and lower extremity strength, plus the Shark Skill and Davies tests.

q: Which of the following best describes instrumental support?
o: Tangible, practical help such as transport or childcare
e: Instrumental support is practical and tangible. The other three are emotional, informational and companionship support.

q: All of the following are examples of behaviour strategies except:
e: Positive self-talk is a cognitive strategy, as are imagery and the stopping technique. Behavioural strategies change actions and habits.

q: In SMART goals, how is realistic defined?
o: The client is both willing and able to work toward the goal
The goal is specific to one body part
e: Realistic means the client is both willing and able — the goal can actually be achieved.

q: How can a trainer support a client in the action stage?
o: Continue educating them concerning the benefits of exercise
e: In the action stage the client is doing the behaviour; reinforcing why it is worth continuing supports adherence.

q: How is parental support beneficial for clients?
e: Modelling the behaviour is the mechanism.

q: How should a trainer contact a potential client after taking their details?
o: Mail a handwritten card within 24 hours
Wait for the client to make contact
e: A handwritten card within 24 hours.

q: What is the most appropriate way to approach a potential client performing an exercise incorrectly?
o: Telling them you know the right way
Recommending a better way of performing it
Asking if you can make a suggestion
Telling them about a potential benefit of the exercise
e: Leading with a benefit opens the conversation without implying they are doing it wrong.

q: How should a goal for new clients be calculated?
o: Estimate how many potential clients to contact every hour
Calculate sessions per year, then the closing percentage
Calculate sessions per week needed for the monetary goal, how many clients that requires, then a contact timeline
Reach out to five contacts a day until the goal is met
e: Work backwards from the monetary goal to sessions per week, then to clients needed, then to a contact timeline.

q: What is the unique feature of Type IIa muscle fibres?
o: They create energy both aerobically and anaerobically
e: Type IIa are intermediate fibres, drawing on both aerobic and anaerobic pathways.

q: With the internal obliques, what is the main muscular role of the transverse abdominis?
o: To isometrically stabilize the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex
e: Isometric stabilisation of the LPHC, not production of movement.

q: When overtraining occurs, which hormone is typically elevated in the bloodstream?
e: Cortisol rises with prolonged training stress without adequate recovery.
